event: Georg Elser, a Swabian carpenter working alone, sets off the bomb he hid inside a pillar of the Bürgerbräukeller in Munich, thirteen minutes after Hitler left the hall
place: Bürgerbräukeller, Munich, Germany (arrest the same evening in Konstanz, on the Swiss border)
why: A lone carpenter spends more than thirty nights hollowing out a pillar to stop a war, misses Hitler by thirteen minutes, is arrested at the border the same evening, kept alive five years for a show trial, shot at Dachau weeks before the end, and smeared for decades before Germany honored him.
alternates: The five Sullivan brothers of Waterloo, Iowa, all lost when the cruiser USS Juneau was torpedoed after the Naval Battle of Guadalcanal on 13 November 1942; the account's card No. 56 covered them, so an article would need the survivors' days in the water and the family's story to go far beyond it.

Operation Torch, 8 November 1942: American and British troops land in French Morocco and Algeria, the first big American ground operation against the Axis, with Vichy French forces fighting back at Casablanca, Oran and Algiers before a ceasefire.

facts.text: Johann Georg Elser was born on 4 January 1903 in Hermaringen in Württemberg and grew up in nearby Königsbronn, the eldest child of the farmer and timber dealer Ludwig Elser.
It was a hard childhood. His father drank, the family slid into poverty, and Georg had to take responsibility for his five younger brothers and sisters early.
After a broken off apprenticeship at the Königsbronn ironworks, given up for health reasons, he trained as a carpenter and passed his journeyman's exam as the best of his year.
From 1925 he worked for about seven years around Lake Constance, in Germany and Switzerland, including a spell at a clock factory in Konstanz making clock cases, until spring 1930.
He was quiet but sociable: he played the zither and the double bass at local dances, liked hiking, and his girlfriend Mathilde Niedermann bore his only son, Manfred, in 1930.
In 1928 or 1929 he joined the Red Front Fighters' League, the Communist Party's paramilitary arm, but was never an active member. He voted Communist until 1933.
He rejected Nazism from the start. He refused to give the Hitler salute and walked away when Hitler's speeches were played on the radio.
Under interrogation he gave hard numbers for his anger: a carpenter earned 1 Reichsmark an hour in 1929 and only 68 pfennigs now, while the deductions from a much smaller wage had grown.
In the autumn of 1938, during the Sudeten crisis and the Munich Agreement, he concluded that war was coming and decided to kill the Nazi leadership: Hitler, Göring and Goebbels.

On 8 November 1938 he travelled to Munich for the yearly anniversary of Hitler's 1923 putsch. After Hitler's speech he walked into the Bürgerbräukeller hall, saw the lectern, and found that anyone could enter and nobody guarded it.
He watched the Nazi leaders' memorial march on 9 November 1938, the same evening that Goebbels's speech set off the Kristallnacht pogroms, and went home determined to plant a bomb in that hall.
At the Waldenmaier fittings factory in Heidenheim, where he worked from December 1936 to March 1939, he stole 250 pressed black powder pellets and hid them in his wardrobe at home.
At Easter 1939 (he left on 4 April) he went back to Munich, measured the pillar behind the lectern, and sketched it. He tried to get a job at the beer hall, but failed.

From April 1939 he worked at the Vollmer quarry in Königsbronn and stole more than 100 explosive charges and over 125 detonators. After an accident at work in May he gave all his time to the plan, testing detonators in his parents' orchard in July.

He moved to Munich in August 1939. From 1 September he rented a back room from Alfons and Rosa Lehmann at Türkenstrasse 94 for just under 4 marks a week, telling them he was a cabinetmaker and inventor.

His routine: a simple supper in the beer hall between 8 and 10 p.m., then hiding on the gallery until the hall was locked. He worked until 2 or 3 a.m., dozed in his hiding place, and slipped out the back to Kellerstrasse in the morning.

By his own statement he spent 30 to 35 nights inside the hall. The Bundesarchiv and the German Resistance Memorial Center say more than thirty; one postwar author claimed 90, which Hoch called certainly wrong.

He cut a hidden door, about 80 by 80 cm, into the pillar's wooden paneling, wrapped his tools in rags to deaden the noise, worked by a shaded flashlight, and lined the door with 2 mm sheet iron so that a nail or a knock would not give the cavity away.
He caught the rubble in a sack, carried it out in a small suitcase, and tipped it into the river Isar. He finished hollowing the pillar at the end of October.

In early October he was bedridden with a badly inflamed right knee from kneeling at the pillar, and Rosa Lehmann brought him food. Investigators later learned the bomber had worked kneeling, and Huber broke Elser by confronting him with the knee.

His time fuse used two clock mechanisms that could be set up to six days ahead, accurate to within fifteen minutes. When they ran down they released a sliding block that drove nails onto rifle cartridges and fired the charge.

On the night of 2 November he loaded the explosives into the pillar. After a failed try, he fitted the clockwork after midnight on 5 November, following a dance in the hall, and by 6 a.m. on 6 November he had set it for the evening of 8 November.

He took his belongings to his sister Marie Hirth in Stuttgart, telling her only that he had to go over the fence. On the night of 7 November he went back to the empty hall one last time to check that the clocks were running.
Hitler at first meant not to speak at all that year, with the attack in the West pending, and to send Rudolf Hess. He decided only late on 7 November to come.

On 8 November 1939 Hitler arrived at 8:00 p.m., began speaking at 8:10, and stopped at 9:07, much earlier than in past years. The bomb went off at about 9:20 p.m., thirteen minutes after he walked out.

He was hurrying to catch his special train to Berlin, which left Munich at 9:31 p.m. (Wikipedia gives 9:30). Hoch ties the rush to the planned offensive in the West; Wikipedia adds that fog was forecast, ruling out a flight next morning.
The blast shattered the pillar and brought down the ceiling. Where Hitler's lectern had stood was a pile of rubble a meter high.

Eight people died, seven party members and the waitress Maria Henle, and 63 were injured, according to the Bundesarchiv and the Baden Württemberg civic education center. Wikipedia explains the gap: seven died that night and an eighth, Michael Schmeidl, on 13 November. The DHM gives seven dead and over 60 injured, a German Historical Institute caption seven dead and 60 injured, and Wikipedia's summary 62 injured.

At about 8:45 p.m., before the bomb went off, two customs officers arrested Elser in Konstanz, near the Swiss border between the Kreuzlinger Tor and Emmishofer Tor posts. He had stopped to listen to Hitler's speech on a radio.

In his pockets were a picture postcard of the Bürgerbräukeller, a Red Front badge, notes on munitions production and parts of a detonator, and only a few marks. They looked suspicious once news of the blast reached Konstanz.

He was beaten repeatedly in Munich and made a full confession to the special commission on the night of 13 to 14 November 1939. In Berlin the Gestapo questioned him again from 19 to 23 November, in sessions lasting up to 15 hours.

Nazi propaganda blamed British intelligence and Otto Strasser. It tied the bombing to two British agents, Sigismund Payne Best and Richard Stevens, kidnapped at Venlo on 9 November 1939, who had nothing to do with it. Many in the German opposition, and most British and American newspapers, assumed instead that the Nazis had staged it, like the Reichstag fire.

Almost all his relatives were arrested and taken to Berlin, held at the Hotel Kaiserhof, and made to identify him while he bore the marks of torture. The quarry owner he had stolen from spent over a year in a concentration camp.

Hitler wanted a show trial after victory, so Elser was kept as a special prisoner in the cell block at Sachsenhausen (from 1940 according to the memorial center; the Heidenheim Georg Elser working group says early 1941). He had a large cell, a workbench and a zither he built himself, at least two SS guards day and night, and no contact with other prisoners for more than five years.
Early in 1945, probably in February, he was moved to Dachau and kept in solitary confinement in the commandant's arrest block.

On 5 April 1945 Gestapo chief Heinrich Müller wrote to the Dachau commandant that Elser, code named Eller, was to be quietly killed and his death blamed on an air raid. The letter was stamped as received on 9 April.

On 9 April 1945 SS Oberscharführer Theodor Bongartz shot Elser near the old crematorium at Dachau. His body was burned at once and he has no grave. That same day Bonhoeffer, Canaris and others were murdered at Flossenbürg.

After the war, Martin Niemöller claimed on 17 January 1946 that Elser had been an SS man acting on Hitler's personal orders, and Payne Best told a similar story in 1950. His mother fought these claims until her death in 1960, and the family got no compensation.

In 1964 the historian Lothar Gruchmann found the Gestapo interrogation record in the old Reich Justice Ministry files, and Anton Hoch's 1969 study showed Elser had acted alone. Chancellor Helmut Kohl honored him publicly in 1984.

Recognition came late: a plaque in Munich's Gasteig in 1989, the Königsbronn memorial center in 1998, a German stamp for his 100th birthday in 2003, and a 17 meter sculpture of his profile in Berlin in 2011. In Munich a neon memorial lights up every night at 9:20 for one minute.

quotes.text: Through my considerations I came to the conviction that by removing these 3 men, other men would come into government who would make no unbearable demands on foreign countries, "who would not want to take in any foreign land", and who would take care to improve the social conditions of the workers.
quotes.by: Georg Elser, Gestapo interrogation record, Berlin
quotes.note: English translation by WW2 Dispatches research. German original as printed by the Bundesarchiv (BArch R 3001/23100, pp. 106 to 107): Durch meine Überlegungen kam ich zu der Überzeugung, dass durch die Beseitigung dieser 3 Männer andere Männer an die Regierung kommen, die an das Ausland keine untragbaren Forderungen stellen, "die kein fremdes Lande einbeziehen wollen" und die für eine Besserung der sozialen Verhältnisse der Arbeiterschaft Sorge tragen werden.

quotes.text: I also wanted to prevent by my act even greater bloodshed.
quotes.by: Georg Elser, Gestapo interrogation record, Berlin
quotes.note: English as given by Wikipedia; the German Resistance Memorial Center quotes the phrase as even greater bloodshed (source 0). German: Ich wollte ja auch durch meine Tat ein noch größeres Blutvergießen verhindern (as cited from J. P. Stern); the Jüdische Allgemeine (source 27) prints it without auch. Use the short form if in doubt.

quotes.text: I considered how to improve the conditions of the workers and avoid a war.
quotes.by: Georg Elser, Gestapo interrogation record, Berlin
quotes.note: English as given by Wikipedia. German as printed in the Jüdische Allgemeine (source 27): Ich stellte Betrachtungen an, wie man die Verhältnisse für die Arbeiterschaft bessern und einen Krieg vermeiden kann. The German Resistance Memorial Center quotes improve workers' conditions and avoid a war (source 2).

quotes.text: that Germany will make still further demands on other countries and annex other countries, and that a war is therefore unavoidable
quotes.by: Georg Elser, Gestapo interrogation record (protocol p. 88)
quotes.note: English translation by WW2 Dispatches research. German as printed by Hoch: daß Deutschland anderen Ländern gegenüber noch weitere Forderungen stellen und sich andere Länder einverleiben wird und daß deshalb ein Krieg unvermeidlich ist. Hoch comments that these lines without doubt came from Elser himself.

quotes.text: I went in through the main entrance on Rosenheimerstrasse, through the cloakroom into the hall, which was empty and unlit. I did not notice that anyone saw me. I saw nobody. The hall door was not locked.
quotes.by: Georg Elser, Gestapo interrogation record, on his last visit to the hall
quotes.note: English translation by WW2 Dispatches research. German as printed by Hoch, p. 407: Durch den Haupteingang in der Rosenheimerstraße ging ich durch den Garderobenraum in den Saal, der leer und unbeleuchtet war. Ich bemerkte nicht, daß ich dabei von irgend jemandem beobachtet worden wäre. Ich habe niemanden gesehen. Die Saaltür war nicht verschlossen.

quotes.text: thereby let the matter take its course.
quotes.by: Georg Elser, Gestapo interrogation record, on setting the clocks on the morning of 6 November
quotes.note: English translation by the German Resistance Memorial Center.

quotes.by: Heinrich Müller, Gestapo chief, first question when Franz Josef Huber phoned him with Elser's confession
quotes.when: November 1939 (recalled by Huber after the war)
quotes.note: English translation by WW2 Dispatches research. German as printed by Hoch, p. 413: Und wer steckt dahinter? Hoch's source is Huber's own account (IfZ ZS 735).

quotes.by: Heinrich Himmler, written in green pencil on the commission's report finding that Elser acted alone
quotes.note: English translation by WW2 Dispatches research. German as printed by Hoch, p. 413: Welcher Idiot hat den Bericht gemacht?

quotes.text: Of course people are whispering that it is a second Reichstag fire, staged by themselves to stir up anger against England. I do not believe that.
quotes.note: English translation by WW2 Dispatches research. German as quoted by Hoch, note 14, from Hassell, Vom anderen Deutschland (1948): Natürlich wird gemunkelt, es sei ein zweiter Reichstagsbrand, also selbst inszeniert, um den Zorn gegen England zu reizen. Ich glaube das nicht.

quotes.text: During one of the next terror attacks on Munich or the area around Dachau, Eller is supposedly fatally injured. To this end I ask that Eller be liquidated in an absolutely inconspicuous way once such a situation arises.
quotes.by: Heinrich Müller, Chief of the Gestapo, letter to the Dachau commandant Eduard Weiter
quotes.note: English translation by WW2 Dispatches research. German as transcribed (spelling errors in the original kept): Bei einem der nächsten Terrorangriffe auf München bezw. auf die Umgebung von Dachau ist angeblich "Eller" tötlich verunglückt. Ich bitte, zu diesem Zweck "Eller" in absolut unauffälliger Weise nach Eintritt einer solchen Situation zu liquidieren. The letter closes: Nach Kenntnisnahme dieses Schreibens und nach Vollzug bitte ich es zu vernichten (After reading this letter and carrying it out, please destroy it). I could not open the University of Amsterdam page directly; the transcription comes from cryptocellar.org, which cites it. Hoch (source 20, note 124) confirms the Schnellbrief of 5 April 1945.

quotes.text: Five years before Stauffenberg, Elser came as close as imaginable to the goal of killing Hitler and so of working against the disaster of war that he clearly foresaw.
quotes.by: Peter Steinbach, historian, scientific director of the German Resistance Memorial Center
quotes.when: interview in the LpB Baden Württemberg Elser dossier
quotes.note: English translation by WW2 Dispatches research. German: Elser kam fünf Jahre vor Stauffenberg dem Ziel denkbar nahe, Hitler zu töten und so dem von ihm klar vorausgesehenen Verhängnis des Krieges entgegenzuhandeln. He continues: Er macht deutlich, dass auch ein Einzelner den Unrechtscharakter eines Regimes erkennen kann (He makes clear that even a single person can recognize a regime's injustice).

quotes.text: I wanted to prevent the war.
quotes.by: Attributed to Georg Elser; title of the German Resistance Memorial Center's Elser exhibition and website
quotes.note: German: Ich habe den Krieg verhindern wollen. Used in quotation marks as the title by the GDW and the LpB, but I did not find the exact protocol passage. Use only as the exhibition's title, not as a verified quote.

photos.caption: The Gestapo photo of Elser released to the press in November 1939, after his capture; for decades it was the image of him the world knew.

photos.caption: The street entrance of the Bürgerbräukeller on Rosenheimer Strasse, Munich, photographed in November 1923 just after Hitler's putsch began there; Elser walked in through this main entrance on many nights in 1939.
photos.credit: Agence Rol, press photo Rol 88245, November 1923; Bibliothèque nationale de France, département Estampes et photographie, EI-13 (1064), Gallica ark:/12148/btv1b53123618d; Wikimedia Commons; public domain (PD-France, anonymous work, expired).
photos.note: Downloaded at 1280 px. Not of 1939, but the building and doorway are the same. Poster beside the door reads Tanz, Konzert.

photos.caption: Hitler at the microphone in the Bürgerbräukeller hall on 8 November 1933, the yearly putsch anniversary; the gallery where Elser later hid each night runs above the crowd.
photos.credit: Uncredited photographer, agency Robert Sennecke, Internationaler Illustrations Verlag Berlin; Narodowe Archiwum Cyfrowe (National Digital Archives of Poland), sygn. 3/1/0/17/12303/4; Wikimedia Commons; public domain (tagged public domain by the NAC; CC0 on Commons).
photos.note: Downloaded at 1280 px; the NAC caption bar at the bottom was cropped off. Hess, Göring, Frank and Streicher are among those named on the file page; I have not checked each face.

photos.caption: Hitler among the party veterans in the Bürgerbräukeller at the putsch anniversary of November 1938, the gathering Elser came to Munich to scout.
photos.credit: Unidentified press photographer, November 1938; Narodowe Archiwum Cyfrowe (National Digital Archives of Poland), sygn. 3/1/0/17/12306/2; Wikimedia Commons; public domain (PD-Poland).
photos.note: Downloaded at 1280 px; NAC caption bar cropped off. The NAC dates it 9 November 1938, but the beer hall gathering was on the evening of 8 November, so say November 1938. Goebbels (left, seated) and Hess (right foreground) are named on the file page.
